Title: Diagnosis
Details:
- What the test does:
  - It creates a cpio archive with two entries (test1.xml, test2.xml) using ArchiveStreamFactory/ArchiveOutputStream.
  - It then reads the archive back via ArchiveStreamFactory/ArchiveInputStream and iterates entries with getNextEntry(), copying each entry’s content via IOUtils.copy(in, out).

- Where the failure occurs:
  - The reported failure is an unexpected EOF while unpacking a CPIO archive. In the reader, CpioArchiveInputStream.getNextEntry() delegates to getNextCPIOEntry(), which immediately starts reading the next header using readFully (first 2 bytes of magic, possibly 4 more for the full magic string).
  - readFully throws EOFException if the underlying stream returns -1 before the requested number of bytes are read.

- Why the stream is at the wrong position (root cause):
  - At the end of each file’s content, CpioArchiveInputStream.read(byte[], int, int) detects that entryBytesRead == entry.getSize() and then:
    - applies data padding via pad(entry.getSize(), 4) for the new ASCII format (or 2 for old binary),
    - sets entryEOF = true,
    - returns -1 to signal end-of-entry.
  - The pad method is implemented using a single call to InputStream.skip for the needed number of padding bytes:
    - pad(count, border) computes how many bytes to skip and calls this.in.skip(border - (count % border)) exactly once.
    - However, InputStream.skip is not guaranteed to skip the requested number of bytes in a single call; it may skip fewer bytes (including 0) even when not at EOF. The current implementation doesn’t loop to ensure all padding bytes are consumed.

- How this causes EOF later:
  - During IOUtils.copy(in, out) for the first entry, CpioArchiveInputStream.read() reaches the end of the entry’s data and calls pad(), but due to the non-robust skip, it may leave 1–3 padding bytes unread.
  - After IOUtils.copy returns, the while-loop asks for the next entry. getNextCPIOEntry() first calls closeEntry() if a previous entry exists. But since entryEOF was already set by read() when it returned -1, closeEntry()’s read-loop immediately sees -1 and exits, consuming nothing further. Any leftover padding bytes remain.
  - getNextCPIOEntry() then attempts to read the next header’s magic via readFully. It reads the remaining padding bytes instead of header bytes. Depending on how many bytes are left and where in the file we are:
    - It may construct an invalid magic and then fail, or
    - More commonly, readFully runs out of input while trying to fetch the complete magic/header and throws EOFException.
  - This matches the reported “unexpected EOF” both for archives created by the library and by external tools (e.g., macOS cpio), because the reader’s pad logic is the culprit, not the writer.

- Additional observations:
  - Handling of the TRAILER!!! entry (end-of-archive marker) won’t be reached if the stream is misaligned by leftover padding, which explains EOF rather than a clean null return from getNextEntry().
  - There is also a minor bug in CRC accumulation (summing b[pos] instead of b[off + pos]) that could cause “CRC Error” in CRC-enabled archives; however, it is unrelated to the EOF symptom in this test.

- Conclusion:
  - The unexpected EOF stems from CpioArchiveInputStream.pad not reliably consuming all required padding bytes because it uses a single, unchecked InputStream.skip call. This leaves the stream misaligned for the next header read, causing readFully in getNextCPIOEntry to throw EOFException. The failure in testCpioUnarchive is a direct manifestation of this misalignment after copying the first entry’s data.

Based on the available information, provide the signatures of the most likely culprit methods for the bug. Your answer will be processed automatically, so make sure to only answer with the accurate signatures of all likely culprits (in `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` format), without commentary (one per line).
